title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files

reading.body:
This incident shows a general-purpose AI coding tool being used as an active component in offensive cyber operations. The Aurora ransomware group used Cursor Agent, which runs on Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation attacks against target organizations. The tool was not compromised or manipulated in a technical sense, it was simply operated by attackers as a productivity aid for conducting intrusions, placing it in the category of a legitimate system used outside the conditions it was built for.

The failure sits at the access and policy layer rather than in the model's outputs. Cursor Agent was apparently reachable by actors who then directed it toward exploitation tasks. Catching this kind of misuse would require either behavioral monitoring that flags attack-pattern queries, access controls that limit who can use the tool for what purposes, or both. Neither control is described as having been in place.

What is not established is whether Cursor or Anthropic had prior knowledge of this use, whether the tools produced outputs that would have been refused under stated policies, or whether any of the affected organizations have confirmed the reported intrusions. The findings come from threat intelligence researchers, and no independent verification or legal determination is reported.

reports.title: Russian-speaking cybercriminals used SpaceX’s Cursor AI tool to hack seven companies
Aurora ransomware targets ESXi, abuses Cursor Agent for exploitation

summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that the Aurora ransomware group has been active since April 2026 and is targeting organizations across multiple countries. The group operates a data leak site and has developed a Linux ransomware variant specifically designed to attack ESXi virtualization environments. Between April and May 2026, Aurora operators used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation attacks against ten target organizations. The ESXi ransomware uses ChaCha20 encryption and includes specialized features to kill running virtual machines, encrypt virtual disk files, and leave the hypervisor bootable so victims can read ransom demands.

In a separate discovery, researchers identified a second Aurora operation cluster with medium confidence, affecting eight victim organizations across multiple countries including Israel, Germany, Austria, Spain, the United States, and Argentina. This cluster used different attack methods, including exploiting SQL Server vulnerabilities and extracting data to self-hosted storage. Gambit Security published technical indicators and command-line details of the Aurora encryptor to help organizations identify and defend against these threats.
